title: Robotics, world models & control
summary: Connect perception and prediction to physical action under uncertainty.
html:
Connect perception and prediction to physical action under uncertainty.

The embodied loop

A robot senses the environment, estimates state, chooses a plan, and executes control actions. Sensors are noisy and delayed. Coordinate frames, calibration, and time synchronization determine whether observations can be combined. A correct object label does not by itself provide a safe grasp pose.

Control operates at multiple timescales

A high-level planner may choose a destination while a lower-level controller stabilizes motion. Feedback compares desired and measured state. Model predictive control repeatedly optimizes a finite horizon and executes only the next action before observing again. Latency and actuator limits constrain feasible behavior.

Learned policies and world models

Imitation learning copies demonstrations; RL optimizes through interaction; world models predict state or observation transitions. Learned dynamics can support planning but suffer compounding error over rollouts. Simulator success requires validation under real sensor, friction, lighting, and contact conditions.

Evaluate physical robustness

Test recovery, perturbations, new objects, and environment changes. Record collisions, near misses, control saturation, and operator interventions, not only completion rate. Separate a model’s suggested action from the system authorized to actuate hardware.

Worked example

A controller running at 100 Hz has 10 ms per cycle. A model taking 250 ms cannot directly supply every control update at that rate. A system may use the model for slower plans and a separate real-time controller for stabilization.

What goes wrong

A video demonstration shows one trajectory, not reliability across the operating envelope. Reset conditions and human interventions can hide failure modes.

Check your understanding

Why replan after each action in model predictive control?

Reveal the explanation

New observations correct state estimates and reduce dependence on long, potentially inaccurate open-loop predictions.

How the pieces connect

A usable chapter has a flow of decisions, evidence, and checks. Use this diagram as a navigation aid, then test each step on a small real example.

An operating model for robotics, world models & control

Robotics turns model error into physical consequences. A learned perception model may be one component of a safety-critical loop, but it cannot replace coordinate calibration, actuator limits, collision handling, control timing, and recovery. High-level reasoning and low-level control typically operate at very different rates.

The diagram is deliberately sequential, but real systems loop. A surprising result may expose a bad representation; a production incident may reveal a missing evaluation slice; a performance limit may require an algorithmic change. The point is to preserve the link between the abstract concept, the evidence you observe, and the decision you make next.

Field guide: four decisions in order

1. Sense

Sense establishes the next constraint. Synchronize calibrated observations and state estimates. Begin by making the object of study explicit. A vague input, target, or operating condition creates ambiguity that later computation cannot repair.

Write down the input boundary and the unit of analysis. This makes it possible to distinguish a missing fact from a mismatch between the question and the data or system.

2. Plan

Plan establishes the next constraint. Choose a target or trajectory under constraints. Now make the mechanism inspectable. Prefer a small run whose intermediate values, examples, or traces can be examined before you automate a larger workflow.

Keep a concrete artifact: a small dataset, a notebook cell, a trace, a benchmark command, or a hand-worked calculation. It is the fastest way to surface hidden assumptions.

3. Control

Control establishes the next constraint. Close feedback loops within real-time deadlines. Treat the first result as a measurement, not a conclusion. Compare it with a baseline and vary one assumption at a time so that the observed change has an interpretable cause.

Check a deliberately awkward case alongside the happy path. Boundary conditions, rare examples, and resource limits reveal more than another aggregate score.

4. Recover

Recover establishes the next constraint. Detect uncertainty, stop safely, and replan. Finish by connecting the result to a real choice. Record the operating range, uncertainty, and the condition under which the next person should stop, escalate, or revisit the earlier steps.

Preserve the decision record with the result. A useful technical chapter leaves enough context for a reader to reproduce the reasoning, challenge it, and choose a safe next action.

When the first approach fails

Do not respond to a weak result by immediately adding scale, complexity, or another framework. First locate the failure: the input may not match the intended problem; the representation may discard a useful signal; the measurement may reward the wrong outcome; or the system may have crossed a memory, latency, reliability, or authority boundary. Change one layer, repeat the smallest useful check, and keep the before-and-after evidence.

Gotcha. A polished output can hide an untested assumption. The most convincing demonstration is a counterexample the workflow handles deliberately, with the limitation stated in the release or research record.

A rigorous way to practice

  1. Sense. Synchronize calibrated observations and state estimates.
  2. Plan. Choose a target or trajectory under constraints.
  3. Control. Close feedback loops within real-time deadlines.
  4. Recover. Detect uncertainty, stop safely, and replan.

Test the complete loop under perturbations: latency, missing observations, lighting changes, object variation, contact, and emergency stop. Record near misses and interventions, not only successful completions.

Questions that keep the chapter honest

AskWhy it mattersEvidence to collect
What assumptions does this method make?Every method encodes a view of data, hardware, or behavior.Inputs, representations, constraints, and cases outside the expected range.
What would make the result fail?Failure modes show where an aggregate result is fragile.Boundary cases, counterexamples, slices, and perturbations.
What decision changes if it improves?A metric only matters through an operational action.Baseline, threshold, cost, latency, and human-review consequences.
